evidence: PUCRS identifies its professor Charles Monteiro as author of Porto Alegre e suas escritas. However, b has only a name and CAPES numeric identifier, with no works or affiliation; I could not independently connect that identifier to the author.
Contexto identifies the author of História oral e memória and História, metodologia, memória as a professor of Brazilian history at UFPE, matching the UFPE repository-supervisor anchor.

The 1991 thesis on gendered portrayals of saints in Italian hagiography connects closely to Gendered Voices (1999). Boston College confirms Catherine M. Mooney has a Yale medieval-history PhD and lists both Gendered Voices and Philippine Duchesne among her books.

Edinburgh explicitly associates this ORCID with Aaron William Moore, whose 2006 Princeton thesis studied servicemen and war diaries. Aaron Stephen Moore wrote the 2006 Cornell thesis on imperial technology that became Constructing East Asia; these are distinct careers.

The Technological Imaginary of Imperial Japan (2006) is Aaron Stephen Moore’s Cornell dissertation. ASU confirms that his Cornell dissertation on technology and imperial visions became Constructing East Asia, directly connecting the thesis and book.

Paco identifies the author of As transformações dos espaços públicos as UERJ historian Marco Morel. However, b supplies no works or affiliation, and its CAPES numeric identifier could not be independently connected to that author.

Paco identifies the author of As transformações dos espaços públicos as a professor in UERJ’s history department and graduate program, matching the repository-supervisor anchor. It also clarifies that O golpe começou em Washington was written by Edmar Morel and later edited by Marco.

Rutgers confirms Karl F. Morrison earned his Cornell PhD in 1961 and began his research in early medieval political and church thought. This matches the 1961 dissertation on Frankish political thought, 814–887, and fits his 1936 birth date.

The Culture of Pain author was an English professor at Iowa, also author of Alexander Pope. The archaeology review is credited to the McGregor Museum archaeologist in Kimberley, South Africa; its disciplinary and institutional career is distinct from the literary and medical-humanities author.

Oklahoma’s dissertation record identifies the 1965 heat-theory author as Robert James Morris. This history-of-science dissertation belongs to a different author from Robert Charles Morris, whose work concerns freedmen’s education and New Jersey historical collections.

Loyola identifies the author of the 1974 Essex-in-Ireland dissertation as Robert E. Morris. His Elizabethan military-history dissertation is distinct from Robert Charles Morris’s work on freedmen’s education and New Jersey collections.

The supplied 1976 thesis and book share the distinctive Reading, Writing and Reconstruction title and the exact subject of freedmen’s education in the South, 1865–70. Chicago’s publisher page confirms Robert C. Morris as author of the resulting book.

A WVU-hosted scholarly article identifies the 1964 Wheeling Daily Intelligencer dissertation as Robert L. Morris’s WVU PhD. This is a different author from Robert Charles Morris, born in 1942, whose distinctive work is Reading, Writing and Reconstruction.

The 2007 UFPE thesis explicitly describes its author’s earlier coauthorship of Cripto maranhenses e seu legado (p. 179) and lists Família e fortuna no Maranhão Colônia (2006) in its bibliography (p. 185), directly linking the dissertation author to both books.
